claim: Diatoms form massive blooms and are central to biogeochemical cycling of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and silica.
source: They form massive blooms and are thus central to the biogeochemical cycling of important elements such as carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and silica, in addition to their important role at the base of marine food webs (Armbrust, 2009; Nelson et al., 1995; Morel and Price, 2003; Strass and Nöthig, 1996; Tréguer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to five published works (Armbrust, 2009; Nelson et al., 1995; Morel and Price, 2003; Strass and Nöthig, 1996; Tréguer et al., 2018).

claim: Diatoms are exposed to stress from different biotic and abiotic origins including grazing, viruses, bacteria, allelopathic interactions, light availability, and nutrient limitations.
source: They are exposed to stress from different biotic and abiotic origins such as grazing, viruses, bacteria, allelopathic interactions, light availability, and nutrient limitations (Bidle, 2015; Bidle, 2016; Ianora et al., 2006; Thamatrakoln et al., 2013; Thamatrakoln et al., 2012; Kimura and Tomaru, 2015; van Tol et al., 2017; Vardi et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to eight published works (Bidle, 2015; Bidle, 2016; Ianora et al., 2006; Thamatrakoln et al., 2013; Thamatrakoln et al., 2012; Kimura and Tomaru, 2015; van Tol et al., 2017; Vardi et al., 2006).

claim: Induction of programmed cell death (PCD) in response to different stressors has been suggested as an important mechanism contributing to the fast turnover of phytoplankton and rapid bloom demise.
source: Importantly, induction of programmed cell death (PCD) in response to different stressors has been suggested as an important mechanism contributing to the fast turnover of phytoplankton and the rapid bloom demise (Bidle, 2015; Bidle, 2016; Vardi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published works (Bidle, 2015; Bidle, 2016; Vardi et al., 2007).

claim: Diatoms can differentially respond to diverse environmental cues based on compartmentalized redox fluctuations that also mediate stress-induced PCD.
source: Recent studies suggested that diatoms can differentially respond to diverse environmental cues based on compartmentalized redox fluctuations that also mediate stress-induced PCD (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Rosenwasser et al., 2014; Volpert et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published works (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Rosenwasser et al., 2014; Volpert et al., 2018).

claim: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) play an important role in sensing stress and additional signals across kingdoms, from bacteria to plants and animals.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are known to play an important role in sensing stress and additional signals across kingdoms, from bacteria to plants and animals (Vardi et al., 1999; Mittler et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2012; D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007; Dietz et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to five published works (Vardi et al., 1999; Mittler et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2012; D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007; Dietz et al., 2016).

claim: ROS are produced as byproducts of oxygen-based metabolism in respiration and photosynthesis, by ROS generating enzymes, and due to various stress conditions.
source: They are produced as byproducts of oxygen-based metabolism in respiration and photosynthesis, by ROS generating enzymes, and due to various stress conditions (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007; Sheyn et al., 2016; Foyer and Noctor, 2016; Luo et al., 2014; Vardi et al., 2002; Waring et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to seven published works (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007; Sheyn et al., 2016; Foyer and Noctor, 2016; Luo et al., 2014; Vardi et al., 2002; Waring et al., 2010).

claim: Cells harbor various ROS scavenging enzymes and small antioxidant molecules that regulate and buffer ROS levels, such as glutathione (GSH), ascorbate and NADPH.
source: To maintain redox balance and avoid oxidative damage, cells harbor various ROS scavenging enzymes and small antioxidant molecules that regulate and buffer ROS levels, such as glutathione (GSH), ascorbate and NADPH.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cellular redox regulation.

claim: ROS can cause rapid post-translational modifications of pre-existing proteins through oxidation, affecting their activity faster than changes in gene expression.
source: ROS can cause rapid post-translational modifications of pre-existing proteins through oxidation, affecting their activity faster than changes in gene expression (D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007).

claim: The specificity of the ROS signal is derived from the specific chemical species, its concentration, sub-cellular localization, temporal dynamics, and available downstream ROS-sensitive targets.
source: The specificity of the ROS signal is derived from the specific chemical species, its concentration, sub-cellular localization, temporal dynamics, and available downstream ROS-sensitive targets (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007; Sheyn et al., 2016; Noctor and Foyer, 2016; Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009; Tsukagoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to six published works (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007; Sheyn et al., 2016; Noctor and Foyer, 2016; Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009; Tsukagoshi et al., 2010).

claim: H2O2 is a relatively mild and stable ROS that can accumulate in cells due to various stress conditions and often serves as a signaling molecule.
source: H2O2 is a relatively mild and stable ROS that can accumulate in cells due to various stress conditions, thus often serves as a signaling molecule (Vardi et al., 1999; Mittler et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2012; D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007; Dietz et al., 2016; Exposito-Rodriguez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to six published works (Vardi et al., 1999; Mittler et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2012; D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007; Dietz et al., 2016; Exposito-Rodriguez et al., 2017).

claim: H2O2 has preferential activity towards cysteine residues and can remodel the redox-sensitive proteome network.
source: It has a preferential activity towards cysteine residues, and can remodel the redox-sensitive proteome network (Rosenwasser et al., 2014; Dietz et al., 2016; Noctor and Foyer, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published works (Rosenwasser et al., 2014; Dietz et al., 2016; Noctor and Foyer, 2016).

claim: H2O2 can diffuse across membranes (depending on membrane properties) and through aquaporin channels.
source: In addition, H2O2 can diffuse across membranes (depending on membrane properties) and through aquaporins channels (Bienert and Chaumont, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (Bienert and Chaumont, 2014).

claim: H2O2 application in marine diatoms led to oxidation patterns similar to other environmental stressors such as nutrient limitations, toxic infochemicals and high light.
source: Importantly, H2O2 application in marine diatoms led to oxidation patterns similar to other environmental stressors such as nutrient limitations, toxic infochemicals and high light, demonstrating that it induces similar physiological responses within the cell (Figure 1) (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Rosenwasser et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published works (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Rosenwasser et al., 2014) and by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: H2O2 concentrations used in these studies were higher than measured in bulk seawater, which is typically in the nanomolar range.
source: Although the H2O2 concentrations used in these studies were higher than measured in bulk seawater, which is typically in the nanomolar range (Zinser, 2018), local concentrations at the microenvironment of phytoplankton can be significantly higher due to patchiness in time and space (Stocker, 2012; Chrachri et al., 2018; Seymour et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four published works (Zinser, 2018; Stocker, 2012; Chrachri et al., 2018; Seymour et al., 2017).

claim: Local and temporal production of H2O2 by the cell itself or by its neighbors could lead to intracellular concentrations which are orders of magnitude higher than measured in bulk seawater in the field.
source: Local and temporal production of H2O2 by the cell itself or by its neighbors could lead to intracellular concentrations which are orders of magnitude higher than measured in bulk seawater in the field, especially during dense blooms or in aggregates and biofilms (Diaz et al., 2018; Diaz et al., 2013; Stocker, 2012; Chrachri et al., 2018; Seymour et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to five published works (Diaz et al., 2018; Diaz et al., 2013; Stocker, 2012; Chrachri et al., 2018; Seymour et al., 2017).

claim: H2O2 application in the model diatom P. tricornutum led to the induction of cell death in a dose-dependent manner, with characteristics of PCD including externalization of phosphatidylserine, DNA laddering, and compromised cell membrane.
source: H2O2 application in the model diatom P. tricornutum also led to the induction of cell death, in a dose-dependent manner, with characteristics of PCD that included externalization of phosphatidylserine, DNA laddering, and compromised cell membrane (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015).

claim: Early oxidation of the mitochondrial GSH pool preceded subsequent cell death at the population level following exposure to H2O2 or diatom-derived infochemicals.
source: Moreover, early oxidation of the mitochondrial GSH pool preceded subsequent cell death at the population level following exposure to H2O2 or diatom-derived infochemicals (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Graff van Creveld et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published works (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Graff van Creveld et al., 2016).

claim: Chloroplast-targeted roGFP (chl-roGFP) exhibited a distinct bimodal distribution following treatments of 50–100 µM H2O2, revealing two distinct subpopulations of 'oxidized' and 'reduced' cells.
source: Chloroplast-targeted roGFP (chl-roGFP) exhibited a distinct bimodal distribution following treatments of 50–100 µM H2O2, revealing two distinct subpopulations of 'oxidized' and 'reduced' cells (Figure 2B–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: The 'oxidized' and 'reduced' subpopulations emerged within the first few minutes after H2O2 addition.
source: These subpopulations emerged within the first few minutes after H2O2 addition (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B–D.

claim: In the 'oxidized' subpopulation, roGFP completely oxidized (~100%) in response to H2O2, reaching a similar distribution of the fully oxidized positive control (200 µM H2O2).
source: In the 'oxidized' subpopulation, roGFP completely oxidized (~100%) in response to H2O2, reaching a similar distribution of the fully oxidized positive control (200 µM H2O2) (Figure 2B–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3G.

claim: In the 'reduced' subpopulation roGFP reached lower values of 30–43% OxD within 2–24 min post treatments, and then gradually recovered.
source: However, in the 'reduced' subpopulation roGFP reached lower values of 30–43% OxD within 2–24 min post treatments, and then gradually recovered (Figure 2B–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3G.

claim: A larger fraction of cells was within the 'oxidized' subpopulation at 20–25 min post treatment compared to later time points, indicating that some cells were able to recover during this time.
source: Interestingly, a larger fraction of cells was within the 'oxidized' subpopulation at 20–25 min post treatment compared to later time points, indicating that some cells were able to recover during this time (Figure 2M).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: The proportion between the 'oxidized' and 'reduced' subpopulations stabilized after 46–51 min post treatment, and was H2O2-dose dependent.
source: The proportion between these subpopulations stabilized after 46–51 min post treatment, and was H2O2-dose dependent, as more cells were within the 'oxidized' subpopulation at higher H2O2 concentrations (Figure 2M).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: Nuclear-targeted roGFP displayed a continuous distribution in response to H2O2 treatments, and no distinct subpopulations could be observed.
source: Nuclear-targeted roGFP displayed a continuous distribution in response to H2O2 treatments, and no distinct subpopulations could be observed (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F–H.

claim: Nuclear roGFP exhibited fast oxidation within minutes post treatment even in response to a low H2O2 concentration of 50 µM.
source: Within minutes post treatment, nuclear roGFP exhibited fast oxidation even in response to a low H2O2 concentration of 50 µM, which had only a mild effect on the chloroplast (Figure 2B,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B,F.

claim: At 50 µM H2O2, nuclear roGFP oxidation was followed by a gradual and much slower recovery, which lasted >5 hr post treatment.
source: At that concentration, nuclear roGFP oxidation was followed by a gradual and much slower recovery, which lasted >5 hr post treatment (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: At higher H2O2 concentrations, the entire population of nuclear roGFP was oxidized within 3 min post treatment, and most cells remained stably oxidized >5 hr post treatment.
source: At higher concentrations, the entire population was oxidized within 3 min post treatment, and most cells remained stably oxidized >5 hr post treatment (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G–H.

claim: The mitochondria-targeted roGFP exhibited a heterogeneous redox response in the 80 µM and 100 µM H2O2 treatments starting at ~24 min post treatment.
source: The mitochondria-targeted roGFP exhibited a heterogeneous redox response, as seen in the 80 µM and 100 µM H2O2 treatments starting at ~24 min post treatment (Figure 2K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2K–L.

claim: Distinct subpopulations in mitochondria-targeted roGFP were not clearly separated until later stages, and were not detected consistently in different experiments.
source: However, distinct subpopulations were not clearly separated until later stages, and were not detected consistently in different experiments (Figure 2K–L and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2K–L and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The fraction of 'oxidized' cells 1–2 hr post treatment was correlated with the fraction of dead cells at 24 hr (R2 = 0.89, p=2.2·10−16).
source: The fraction of 'oxidized' cells 1–2 hr post treatment was correlated with the fraction of dead cells at 24 hr (Figure 3A, R2 = 0.89, p=2.2·10−16), suggesting that early oxidation in the chloroplast in distinct subpopulations may predict cell fate at much later stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, including statistical analysis (R2 = 0.89, p=2.2·10−16).

claim: When sorted 30 min post treatment, the 'oxidized' subpopulation exhibited a high survival rate (92.3 ± 1.4%) that was similar to the 'reduced' subpopulation (94.1 ± 1.1%, p=0.24, paired t-test).
source: When sorted 30 min post treatment, the 'oxidized' subpopulation exhibited a high survival rate (92.3 ± 1.4%) that was similar to the 'reduced' subpopulation (94.1 ± 1.1%, p=0.24, paired t-test) and to sorted untreated control (96 ± 0.9%, p=0.29, Dunnett test, Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, including statistical analysis (p=0.24, paired t-test; p=0.29, Dunnett test).

claim: At later time-points the survival of the 'oxidized' subpopulation gradually diminished, and was significantly lower than both the 'reduced' and control sorted cells (p<0.001 for all comparisons).
source: However, at later time-points the survival of the 'oxidized' subpopulation gradually diminished, and was significantly lower than both the 'reduced' and control sorted cells (p<0.001 for all comparisons, paired t-test for comparisons with 'reduced' cells, Dunnett test for comparisons with control).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, including statistical analysis (p<0.001 for all comparisons).

claim: When sorted 60 min post treatment almost half of the 'oxidized' cells recovered (45.1 ± 2%), but when sorted 100 min following treatment only 12.7 ± 2.1% survived (p<0.001, Tukey test).
source: When sorted 60 min post treatment almost half of the 'oxidized' cells recovered (45.1 ± 2%), but when sorted 100 min following treatment only 12.7 ± 2.1% survived (p<0.001, Tukey test, Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, including statistical analysis (p<0.001, Tukey test).

claim: The 'reduced' subpopulation exhibited a high survival rate similar to the control at all time-points examined (P≥0.86 for all comparisons, Dunnett test).
source: In contrast, the 'reduced' subpopulation from the same culture and treatment exhibited a high survival rate similar to the control at all time-points examined, demonstrating its resilience to the stress (Figure 3B, P≥0.86 for all comparisons, Dunnett test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, including statistical analysis (P≥0.86 for all comparisons, Dunnett test).

claim: There is a distinct phase of 'pre-commitment' to cell death, ranging approximately 30–60 min in most cells, during which despite the strong oxidation in the chloroplast the fate of the 'oxidized' subpopulation is still reversible upon removal of the stress.
source: In addition, we detected a distinct phase of 'pre-commitment' to cell death, ranging approximately 30–60 min in most cells, during which despite the strong oxidation in the chloroplast the fate of the 'oxidized' subpopulation is still reversible upon removal of the stress, and they are still able to survive.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 3B, where survival rates differ between 30 min and later time points.

claim: After the initial 'pre-commitment' phase, the 'oxidized' cells were not able to survive even when the stress was removed from the system by sorting into fresh media.
source: After this initial phase, the 'oxidized' cells were not able to survive even when the stress was removed from the system by sorting into fresh media.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 3B, where survival rates of 'oxidized' cells decrease at later time points.

claim: The distinct 'oxidized' and 'reduced' subpopulations were detected following 80 µM H2O2 treatment in microfluidics experiments, similar to the flow cytometry experiments.
source: We detected the distinct 'oxidized' and 'reduced' subpopulations following 80 µM H2O2 treatment, similar to the flow cytometry experiments (Figure 4C,F, and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C,F and Video 1.

claim: No clear differences were observed in chl-roGFP OxD between the subpopulations prior to treatment.
source: However, no clear differences were observed in their OxD prior to treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Video 1.

claim: The separation between the subpopulations emerged within 20 min of exposure to 80 µM H2O2, and remained stable over the course of the experiment with the 'oxidized' subpopulation maintaining a high OxD above 80%.
source: The separation between the subpopulations emerged within 20 min of exposure to 80 µM H2O2, and remained stable over the course of the experiment with the 'oxidized' subpopulation maintaining a high OxD above 80% (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and Video 1.

claim: The 'reduced' subpopulation exhibited an immediate response to H2O2 comparable with flow cytometry measurements, from 25–45% OxD before treatment to 30–65% OxD during the first 20 min post 80 µM H2O2 treatment.
source: The 'reduced' subpopulation exhibited an immediate response to H2O2 comparable with flow cytometry measurements, from 25–45% OxD before treatment to 30–65% OxD during the first 20 min post 80 µM H2O2 treatment (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, and Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and Video 1.

claim: Following the initial oxidation, the 'reduced' cells recovered gradually over the next hours, reducing to 5–25% OxD 8 hr post treatment, even below the initial basal state.
source: Following this initial oxidation, the 'reduced' cells recovered gradually over the next hours, reducing to 5–25% OxD 8 hr post treatment, even below the initial basal state (Figure 4F, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and Video 1.

claim: A gradual slow reduction was also observed in control cells over the course of the experiment, which may represent acclimation to the experimental setup or a diurnal redox alteration.
source: A gradual slow reduction was also observed in control cells over the course of the experiment (Figure 4E, Video 2), which may represent acclimation to the experimental setup or a diurnal redox alteration.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and Video 2, with speculation about the cause.

claim: Control cells did not oxidize in response to addition of fresh media, excluding the possibility that the oxidation observed in 80 µM H2O2 treated cells was due to shear stress during treatment.
source: Control cells did not oxidize in response to addition of fresh media (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), excluding the possibility that the oxidation observed in 80 µM H2O2 treated cells was due to shear stress during treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Cells that exhibited high chl-roGFP oxidation within the first 40 min also died at a much later stage, while cells that maintained a lower OxD were able to recover.
source: We detected a clear correlation between initial oxidation in the chloroplast in response to oxidative stress and subsequent cell fate (Figure 4A–G). Cells that exhibited high chl-roGFP oxidation within the first 40 min also died at a much later stage, while cells that maintained a lower OxD were able to recover (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–G.

claim: Cells of the 'reduced' subpopulation and of control treatment were able to proliferate, further demonstrating their viability under these conditions.
source: In addition, cells of the 'reduced' subpopulation and of control treatment were able to proliferate, further demonstrating their viability under these conditions (Videos 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Videos 1–2.

claim: Logistic regression modeling of cell death as a function of chl-roGFP OxD at 40 min post treatment revealed a threshold of ~74% OxD, which discriminated with high accuracy (98.8%) between cells that subsequently died and cells that survived the treatment.
source: Logistic regression modeling of cell death as a function of chl-roGFP OxD at this time-point revealed a threshold of ~74% OxD, which discriminated with high accuracy (98.8%) between cells that subsequently died and cells that survived the treatment (0.8% false positive, 1.7% false negative; Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 3, including statistical modeling.

claim: The two distinct subpopulations were detected in all the clones measured, and the fraction of the 'oxidized' subpopulation was again correlated with cell death.
source: The two distinct subpopulations were detected in all the clones measured, and the fraction of the 'oxidized' subpopulation was again correlated with cell death (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The different subpopulations observed did not originate from genetic differences, but rather represent phenotypic variability within isogenic populations.
source: Therefore, the different subpopulations observed did not originate from genetic differences, but rather represent phenotypic variability within isogenic populations.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the clonal population experiments shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sorted 'oxidized' subpopulation had a higher fraction of cells at G1 (86.9 ± 1.8%) compared to control untreated cells (76.8 ± 0.7%, p=0.0024, Tukey test).
source: The sorted 'oxidized' subpopulation had a higher fraction of cells at G1 (86.9 ± 1.8%) compared to control untreated cells (76.8 ± 0.7%, p=0.0024, Tukey test, Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6, including statistical analysis (p=0.0024, Tukey test).

claim: The 'reduced' subpopulation had a smaller fraction of G1 cells (68.7 ± 2.2%) compared to both control (p=0.011, Tukey test) and 'oxidized' cells (p=0.0001, paired t-test), and exhibited a larger fraction of G2/M cells.
source: The 'reduced' subpopulation on the other hand had a smaller fraction of G1 cells (68.7 ± 2.2%) compared to both control (p=0.011, Tukey test) and 'oxidized' cells (p=0.0001, paired t-test), and exhibited a larger fraction of G2/M cells (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6, including statistical analysis (p=0.011, Tukey test; p=0.0001, paired t-test).

claim: Cell cycle phase alone cannot explain the differences between the subpopulations, but it is linked to the chloroplast EGSH response to oxidative stress and may represent an important factor that affects H2O2 sensitivity in the population.
source: These results demonstrate that although cell cycle phase alone cannot explain the differences between the subpopulations, it is linked to the chloroplast EGSH response to oxidative stress and may represent an important factor that affects H2O2 sensitivity in the population.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The transition to the dark caused an immediate oxidation of the basal chl-roGFP OxD (without H2O2 treatment), reaching a peak within 15 min.
source: The transition to the dark caused an immediate oxidation of the basal chl-roGFP OxD (without H2O2 treatment), reaching a peak within 15 min (Figure 7A,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A,D.

claim: While still under dark, chl-roGFP gradually reduced while maintaining a continuous distribution.
source: Then, while still under dark, chl-roGFP gradually reduced while maintaining a continuous distribution (Figure 7A,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A,D.

claim: Upon shifting back to the light, chl-roGFP reduced within 2 min back to its basal state prior to dark exposure.
source: Upon shifting back to the light, chl-roGFP reduced within 2 min back to its basal state prior to dark exposure (Figure 7A,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A,D.

claim: The dark mediated oxidation was specific to the chloroplast and was not detected in the nucleus, demonstrating organelle specificity of these redox fluctuations.
source: The dark mediated oxidation was specific to the chloroplast and was not detected in the nucleus (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), demonstrating organelle specificity of these redox fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The transition to the dark eliminated the bimodal pattern of chl-roGFP oxidation in response to H2O2.
source: The transition to the dark eliminated the bimodal pattern of chl-roGFP oxidation in response to H2O2 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: No distinct subpopulations were observed while cells were under darkness even in cells treated with low H2O2 doses.
source: No distinct subpopulations were observed while cells were under darkness even in cells treated with low H2O2 doses (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: The transition to the dark increased H2O2 sensitivity in the entire population, and following treatment of 80 µM H2O2 and transition to the dark chl-roGFP fully oxidized in the entire population and remained stably oxidized even after transition back to the light.
source: The transition to the dark increased H2O2 sensitivity in the entire population, and following treatment of 80 µM H2O2 and transition to the dark chl-roGFP fully oxidized in the entire population and remained stably oxidized even after transition back to the light (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The bimodal pattern was regained only upon transition back to the light, and only at lower doses of 30 µM and 50 µM H2O2, in which some or most cells were able to recover following this transition.
source: The bimodal pattern was regained only upon transition back to the light, and only at lower doses of 30 µM and 50 µM H2O2, in which some or most cells were able to recover following this transition (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 'Dark' treated cultures exhibited higher mortality compared to 'light' treated cells (p≤0.0064 for all pairs in 50–100 µM H2O2 treatments, t-test).
source: In accordance with the higher chl-roGFP oxidation, 'dark' treated cultures also exhibited higher mortality compared to 'light' treated cells (p≤0.0064 for all pairs in 50–100 µM H2O2 treatments, t-test, Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E, including statistical analysis (p≤0.0064 for all pairs in 50–100 µM H2O2 treatments, t-test).

claim: The mechanism generating the bimodal response in the chloroplast is light dependent and plays an important role in cell fate regulation in diatoms.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the mechanism generating the bimodal response in the chloroplast is light dependent and plays an important role in cell fate regulation in diatoms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the dark/light experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: 1.5 hr after exposure to high light (HL) an 'oxidized' subpopulation started to emerge.
source: Indeed, 1.5 hr after exposure to HL an 'oxidized' subpopulation started to emerge (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The fraction of 'oxidized' cells gradually increased over time of HL exposure.
source: The fraction of 'oxidized' cells gradually increased over time of HL exposure (Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A–B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: These subpopulations were not detected in control cells that were kept under low light (LL), nor in cells expressing nuclear targeted roGFP that were exposed to HL, demonstrating the specificity of the redox signal to the chloroplast.
source: These subpopulations were not detected in control cells that were kept under low light (LL, Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1G–H), nor in cells expressing nuclear targeted roGFP that were exposed to HL (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–B), demonstrating the specificity of the redox signal to the chloroplast.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1G–H, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: CFU survival of the 'oxidized' subpopulation gradually decreased over time of HL exposure and was significantly lower than both control and 'reduced' cells (p<0.001 for all comparisons).
source: CFU survival of the 'oxidized' subpopulation gradually decreased over time of HL exposure and was significantly lower than both control and 'reduced' cells (p<0.001 for all comparisons. Tukey test was used for comparison with control, ANCOVA was used for comparison with 'reduced' and for the interaction with exposure time, Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8D, including statistical analysis (p<0.001 for all comparisons).

claim: While most 'oxidized' cells survived ≤3 hr HL exposure (77.3 ± 4.2% CFU survival), longer exposure of >6 hr to HL led to only 3.1 ± 0.9% CFU survival.
source: While most 'oxidized' cells survived ≤3 hr HL exposure (77.3 ± 4.2% CFU survival), longer exposure of >6 hr to HL led to only 3.1 ± 0.9% CFU survival (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The 'reduced' subpopulation in the same HL treatment exhibited high CFU survival of 92.7 ± 3.6%, and maintained high CFU survival at all time-points examined similar to the control (p=0.93, Tukey test).
source: In contrast, the 'reduced' subpopulation in the same HL treatment exhibited high CFU survival of 92.7 ± 3.6%, and maintained high CFU survival at all time-points examined similar to the control (p=0.93, Tukey test, Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8D, including statistical analysis (p=0.93, Tukey test).

claim: When cells were exposed to 6.3 hr HL and then moved to 1 hr LL the separation between the subpopulations became clearer, with almost no cells with intermediate oxidation states.
source: Interestingly, when cells were exposed to 6.3 hr HL and then moved to 1 hr LL the separation between the subpopulations became clearer, with almost no cells with intermediate oxidation states (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1E–F), resembling the response to H2O2 treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1E–F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: High light can generate heterogeneity in ROS accumulation in the chloroplast within diatom populations, leading to differences in survival probability.
source: To conclude, these findings demonstrate that HL can generate heterogeneity in ROS accumulation in the chloroplast within diatom populations, leading to differences in survival probability and likely affecting sensitivity to additional stressors in the marine environment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the high light experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: In diatoms, chloroplast EGSH is involved in sensing specific environmental stress cues and in regulating cell fate.
source: We propose that in diatoms, chloroplast EGSH is involved in sensing specific environmental stress cues and in regulating cell fate (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the manuscript, shown in Figure 9.

claim: The chloroplast is a major source for generation of both ROS and reductive power to generate and recycle NADPH, thioredoxin and GSH.
source: The chloroplast is a major source for generation of both ROS and reductive power to generate and recycle NADPH, thioredoxin and GSH (Dietz et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (Dietz et al., 2016).

claim: In plants, chloroplast-generated ROS were demonstrated to be involved in retrograde signaling from the chloroplast and in hypersensitive response cell death.
source: In plants, chloroplast-generated ROS were demonstrated to be involved in retrograde signaling from the chloroplast and in hypersensitive response cell death (Dietz et al., 2016; Exposito-Rodriguez et al., 2017; Van Aken and Van Breusegem, 2015; Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four published works (Dietz et al., 2016; Exposito-Rodriguez et al., 2017; Van Aken and Van Breusegem, 2015; Liu et al., 2007).

claim: In diatoms, specific stress cues can lead to ROS accumulation and EGSH oxidation in the chloroplast, as was shown in response to nitrogen limitation, the diatom-derived toxic infochemicals cyanogen bromide, and HL.
source: In diatoms, specific stress cues can lead to ROS accumulation and EGSH oxidation in the chloroplast, as was shown in response to nitrogen limitation, the diatom-derived toxic infochemicals cyanogen bromide, and HL (Figure 8A and Figure 1) (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Rosenwasser et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published works (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Rosenwasser et al., 2014) and by data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 1.

claim: High light can lead to ROS accumulation in the chloroplast by generation of singlet oxygen (1O2) in PSII, and by photoreduction of O2 to superoxide (O2-) in PSI, which in turn is rapidly converted to H2O2 by superoxide dismutase (SOD).
source: Specifically, HL can lead to ROS accumulation in the chloroplast by generation of singlet oxygen (1O2) in PSII, and by photoreduction of O2 to superoxide (O2-) in PSI, which in turn is rapidly converted to H2O2 by superoxide dismutase (SOD) (Waring et al., 2010; Exposito-Rodriguez et al., 2017; Asada, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published works (Waring et al., 2010; Exposito-Rodriguez et al., 2017; Asada, 2006).

claim: Analysis of the redox-sensitive proteome in P. tricornutum revealed over-representation of chloroplast-targeted proteins, that were also oxidized to a greater degree under H2O2 treatment as compared to other subcellular compartments.
source: Analysis of the redox-sensitive proteome in P. tricornutum revealed over-representation of chloroplast-targeted proteins, that were also oxidized to a greater degree under H2O2 treatment as compared to other subcellular compartments, further supporting the existence of a redox-based signaling network in the chloroplast (Rosenwasser et al., 2014; Woehle et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published works (Rosenwasser et al., 2014; Woehle et al., 2017).

claim: Early mitochondrial oxidation was shown to precede subsequent cell-death in response to various stress conditions at the population level in P. tricornutum.
source: In P. tricornutum, early mitochondrial oxidation was shown to precede subsequent cell-death in response to various stress conditions at the population level, but the link with chloroplast EGSH was less clear and depended on the specific stress cue (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015).

claim: In another diatom, chloroplast EGSH was shown to mediate changes in oxidative stress sensitivity upon light-dark transitions.
source: In another diatom, chloroplast EGSH was shown to mediate changes in oxidative stress sensitivity upon light-dark transitions (Volpert et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (Volpert et al., 2018).

claim: A recent model in plants suggested possible mitochondria-chloroplast cooperative interactions in the execution of ROS-mediated PCD.
source: A recent model in plants suggested possible mitochondria-chloroplast cooperative interactions in the execution of ROS-mediated PCD (Van Aken and Van Breusegem, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (Van Aken and Van Breusegem, 2015).

claim: There is evidence for energetic coupling of chloroplasts and mitochondria in diatoms, and they use extensive energetic exchanges between these organelles to regulate the ATP/NADPH ratio.
source: In addition, there are evidence for energetic coupling of chloroplasts and mitochondria in diatoms, and they use extensive energetic exchanges between these organelles to regulate the ATP/NADPH ratio (Bailleul et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (Bailleul et al., 2015).

claim: Redox dynamics of both the mitochondria and the chloroplast are involved in cell fate regulation in diatoms.
source: Taken together with the results presented here, we suggest that redox dynamics of both the mitochondria and the chloroplast are involved in cell fate regulation in diatoms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript and cited literature.

claim: Cells that accumulate ROS above a certain threshold are likely to induce cell death with PCD-like hallmarks.
source: We propose that cells that accumulate ROS above a certain threshold are likely to induce cell death with PCD-like hallmarks (Figure 9), as was shown in response to H2O2 (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015) and as observed in the death of the 'oxidized' subpopulation (Figures 3B and 4F-G, and Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented in the manuscript (Figures 3B, 4F-G, and Figure 8D) and cited literature (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015).

claim: Cells that do not cross the ROS threshold are able to recover and acclimate, as in the 'reduced' subpopulation.
source: Cells that do not cross this threshold are able to recover and acclimate, as in the 'reduced' subpopulation (Figures 3B and 4F-G, and Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figures 3B, 4F-G, and Figure 8D.

claim: A 'death threshold' could be detected by early chl-roGFP oxidation.
source: Based on the data from the microfluidics setup, which allowed cell tracking throughout the entire dynamics during exposure to H2O2, we propose that such a 'death threshold' could be detected by early chl-roGFP oxidation (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The balance between the cellular metabolic state, antioxidant capacity, and the magnitude of the applied stress determines whether a cell will cross the 'death threshold'.
source: The balance between the cellular metabolic state, antioxidant capacity, and the magnitude of the applied stress determines whether a cell will cross the 'death threshold', leading to a differential response within the population.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Harsher stress conditions will have a stronger effect on the population, leading to more cells crossing the threshold and exhibiting early oxidation and subsequent cell death.
source: Harsher stress conditions will have a stronger effect on the population, leading to more cells crossing the threshold and exhibiting early oxidation and subsequent cell death, as shown with increasing H2O2 doses (Figure 2M) or prolonged exposure to HL (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 2M and Figure 8B.

claim: Since clonal populations originating from single-cell isolates maintained the bi-stable chloroplast response, the variability does not result from genetic differences but rather from phenotypic plasticity.
source: Since clonal populations originating from single-cell isolates maintained the bi-stable chloroplast response, the variability does not result from genetic differences but rather from phenotypic plasticity (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The combination of factors such as life history, cell cycle phase, cell age, metabolic activity, heterogeneous microenvironment and biological noise results in a distribution of different metabolic states within the population.
source: The combination of factors such as life history (Graff van Creveld et al., 2016; Murik et al., 2014), cell cycle phase (Papagiannakis et al., 2017; Mathis and Ackermann, 2016), cell age (Levy et al., 2012; Radzinski et al., 2018), metabolic activity (Şimşek and Kim, 2018; Campbell et al., 2018), heterogeneous microenvironment (Stocker, 2012) and biological noise (Balaban, 2011; Raj and van Oudenaarden, 2008) results in a distribution of different metabolic states within the population (Ackermann, 2015; Takhaveev and Heinemann, 2018), which could lead to differential sensitivity to oxidative stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published works (Graff van Creveld et al., 2016; Murik et al., 2014; Papagiannakis et al., 2017; Mathis and Ackermann, 2016; Levy et al., 2012; Radzinski et al., 2018; Şimşek and Kim, 2018; Campbell et al., 2018; Stocker, 2012; Balaban, 2011; Raj and van Oudenaarden, 2008; Ackermann, 2015; Takhaveev and Heinemann, 2018).

claim: In yeast, redox-based heterogeneity was linked to proliferation and aging.
source: In yeast for example, redox-based heterogeneity was linked to proliferation and aging (Radzinski et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (Radzinski et al., 2018).

claim: Differences in cell-cycle phase distribution between the subpopulations likely represent pre-existing disparities.
source: Nevertheless, differences in cell-cycle phase distribution between the subpopulations likely represent pre-existing disparities, supporting the latter.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Differences in cell cycle do not completely explain the variability, and are likely to be a contributing factor rather than the source.
source: However, differences in cell cycle do not completely explain the variability, and are likely to be a contributing factor rather than the source, for example by antioxidants oscillations (Papagiannakis et al., 2017; Burhans and Heintz, 2009; Mathis and Ackermann, 2016; Diaz-Vivancos et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and supported by citations to four published works (Papagiannakis et al., 2017; Burhans and Heintz, 2009; Mathis and Ackermann, 2016; Diaz-Vivancos et al., 2015).

claim: The microfluidics experiments showed no clear differences in chl-roGFP OxD between the subpopulations prior to the treatment.
source: In addition, the microfluidics experiments showed no clear differences in chl-roGFP OxD between the subpopulations prior to the treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), demonstrating that the possible pre-existing heterogeneity is not reflected in the chloroplast EGSH basal level, but rather is based on a different parameter that is yet to be identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The antioxidant capacity of a diatom cell depends on photosynthesis-generated NADPH, which is also used for GSH recycling.
source: The antioxidant capacity of a diatom cell depends on photosynthesis-generated NADPH, which is also used for GSH recycling.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cellular redox regulation.

claim: The transition to the dark may have compromised the biosynthesis and recycling of GSH, therefore enhancing sensitivity to oxidative stress.
source: The transition to the dark may have compromised the biosynthesis and recycling of GSH, therefore enhancing sensitivity to oxidative stress, as was shown in another diatom (Volpert et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation supported by a citation to a published work (Volpert et al., 2018).

claim: The source for heterogeneity could be variability in the flux of photosynthesis-derived reductive power, regulating the recycling rates of antioxidants.
source: Taken together, we propose that the source for heterogeneity could be variability in the flux of photosynthesis-derived reductive power, regulating the recycling rates of antioxidants.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fluctuating light conditions are frequent in natural environments due to mixing, shading, the diel cycle, and tide (in coastal and intertidal regions), and may greatly affect diatoms' susceptibility to diverse abiotic stresses and biotic interactions with pathogens.
source: Fluctuating light conditions are frequent in natural environments due to mixing, shading, the diel cycle, and tide (in coastal and intertidal regions), and may greatly affect diatoms' susceptibility to diverse abiotic stresses and biotic interactions with pathogens.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about marine environments and speculation about the implications.

claim: Phenotypic variability can provide an important strategy to cope with fluctuating environments in microbial populations.
source: Phenotypic variability can provide an important strategy to cope with fluctuating environments in microbial populations (Ackermann, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (Ackermann, 2015).

claim: Co-existence of subpopulations with different susceptibilities to specific stressors can be viewed as a 'bet-hedging' strategy of the population, enabling at least a portion of the population to survive unpredicted stress events and subsequently leads to a growth benefit at the population level.
source: Co-existence of subpopulations with different susceptibilities to specific stressors can be viewed as a 'bet-hedging' strategy of the population, enabling at least a portion of the population to survive unpredicted stress events and subsequently leads to a growth benefit at the population level (Schreiber et al., 2016; Sengupta et al., 2017; Levy et al., 2012; Ackermann, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four published works (Schreiber et al., 2016; Sengupta et al., 2017; Levy et al., 2012; Ackermann, 2015).

claim: In diatoms, phenotypic variability in cell size, shape and susceptibility to stress conditions was suggested.
source: In diatoms, phenotypic variability in cell size, shape and susceptibility to stress conditions was suggested (Armbrust, 2009; Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Volpert et al., 2018; De Martino et al., 2011), but until now the experimental setups were not designed to study individuality in stress response.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four published works (Armbrust, 2009; Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Volpert et al., 2018; De Martino et al., 2011).

claim: Resilience to oxidative stress may come with a cost in the ability to sense environmental cues with high precision, as high ROS buffering capacity may mask milder ROS cues.
source: For example, resilience to oxidative stress may come with a cost in the ability to sense environmental cues with high precision, as high ROS buffering capacity may mask milder ROS cues (Woehle et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation supported by a citation to a published work (Woehle et al., 2017).

claim: Redox-based phenotypic variability may provide a rapid and adjustable strategy to cope with unpredicted stress conditions as compared to relying only on genetic diversity.
source: Redox-based phenotypic variability may provide a rapid and adjustable strategy to cope with unpredicted stress conditions as compared to relying only on genetic diversity.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and inference from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The novel approaches developed here provide new insights into individuality in marine phytoplankton, and enable studying dynamic processes at the single-cell level in diatoms and possibly other ecologically relevant microorganisms.
source: The novel approaches developed here provide new insights into individuality in marine phytoplankton, and enable studying dynamic processes at the single-cell level in diatoms and possibly other ecologically relevant microorganisms.
evidence: This claim is based on the methodological contributions of the manuscript.

claim: P. tricornutum accession Pt1 8.6 (CCMP2561) was purchased from the National Center of Marine Algae and Microbiota (NCMA).
source: P. tricornutum accession Pt1 8.6 (CCMP2561 in the Provasoli-Guillard National Center for Culture of Marine Phytoplankton) was purchased from the National Center of Marine Algae and Microbiota (NCMA, formerly known as CCMP).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the source of the biological material.

claim: Cultures were grown in filtered seawater (FSW) supplemented with F/2 media at 18°C with 16:8 hr light:dark cycle and 80 μmol photons m−2 sec−1 light intensity.
source: Cultures were grown in filtered seawater (FSW) supplemented with F/2 media (Guillard and Ryther, 1962) at 18°C with 16:8 hr light:dark cycle and 80 μmol photons m−2 sec−1 light intensity supplied by cool-white LED lights (Edison, New Taipei, Taiwan).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about culture conditions.

claim: Strains expressing roGFP were obtained as described previously.
source: Strains expressing roGFP were obtained as described previously (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Rosenwasser et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations to two published works (Graff van Creveld et al., 2015; Rosenwasser et al., 2014).

claim: The oxidation of roGFP is reversible, and can be quantified using ratiometric fluorescence measurements.
source: The oxidation of roGFP is reversible, and can be quantified using ratiometric fluorescence measurements (Meyer, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (Meyer, 2008).

claim: The roGFP oxidation degree (OxD) reports the redox potential of the GSH pool (EGSH), which represents the balance between GSH and its oxidized form.
source: The roGFP oxidation degree (OxD) reports the redox potential of the GSH pool (EGSH), which represents the balance between GSH and its oxidized form (Meyer, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published work (Meyer, 2008).

claim: roGFP OxD provides an important metabolic readout of the redox state of the cell, and represents the oxidation state of native proteins in the monitored organelles.
source: Therefore, roGFP OxD provides an important metabolic readout of the redox state of the cell, and represents the oxidation state of native proteins in the monitored organelles (Rosenwasser et al., 2014; Meyer, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published works (Rosenwasser et al., 2014; Meyer, 2008).
